correctness.rationale: Use M=(X+Y)/2 and D=(X−Y)/2. Transformation (M,D)→(X,Y) has Jacobian 2^d. Polar D=r u and decompose M=h u+w, w⊥u; signed bisector H=(||X||²−||Y||²)/(2||X−Y||)=h. Ball constraints are ||w||²+(r+|h|)²≤1. Integrating w-slice volume κ_{d−1}[1−(r+|h|)²]^((d−1)/2), radial factor r^(d−1), sphere area dκ_d and sampling normalization κ_d² gives exactly coefficient 2^d dκ_{d−1}/κ_d. Site X cell is z·u≥h, so signed normalized imbalance is −2 κ_{d−1}/κ_d∫_0^h(1−t²)^((d−1)/2)dt. Independently integrated 3D polynomial: f3 normalizes, E[H3²]=1/20, E[I3²]=421/4200. For high dimension, the normalized r density r^(d−1)(1−r²)^((d−1)/2) concentrates at 1/√2. For fixed z, f_d(z/d)/f_d(0)→exp(−√2|z|), f_d(0)/d→1/√2 by Γ-ratios; Scheffé upgrades pointwise density to TV. The cap map T_d(z)=√d I(z/d) has derivative →−√(2/π) and inverse locally uniformly, so density change-of-variables and Scheffé give Laplace scale 1/√π in TV. No finite-dimensional Monte Carlo proves these limits.

final_claim: For two independent volume-uniform sites in the Euclidean unit ball B_d (integer d≥2), the signed bisector displacement H has an exact all-d integral density, and the signed normalized two-cell volume imbalance is its explicit spherical-cap transform. In d=3 f_H(h)=3(4+|h|)(1−|h|)^4/5 and E[I_3^2]=421/4200; as d→∞ both dH and √d I converge in total variation to Laplace laws with scales 1/√2 and 1/√π, respectively.
limitations: Two independent volume-uniform sites inside same unit Euclidean ball, fixed two sites for each d≥2; no general convex body or more-than-two-site claim.
